headline: Race Point slack tide: 38-pound bass on live mackerel, and the mackerel are stacked deep
subhead: The Bay's staying cooler than the Sound this week, and that's exactly why the bass are still eating during daylight out here.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, six-fifteen, we're anchored up on the west side of Race Point in about 55 feet, right where the rip folds over that hard sand edge, and the fishfinder lights up with mackerel from the surface clear down to the bottom. Thick as I've seen them all summer. We dropped a couple down on light jigs just to confirm what we were looking at, and inside of ten minutes we had a livewell full and lines out on balloon rigs, drifting them back into the seam where the moving water meets the slower stuff off the bar. Slack tide was maybe forty minutes off, current easing up, and that's when the rod in the stern corner just loaded over and stayed down. Twenty minutes later we had a 38-pound bass in the net, fat, full of mackerel, exactly where she should've been.

That's the story of the Bay right now, and it's a different story than what's happening south of us. We said last week this stretch would hold up better than Nantucket Sound as the season pushed into the warm stretch, and that's exactly what's playing out. The Sound and the ocean beaches down toward the Vineyard are running warm enough that the bass have gone mostly nocturnal — daytime fish sulking deep, only really turning on after dark. Cape Cod Bay hasn't crossed that threshold. The water out here is still cool enough, especially on the north side around Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars, that we're getting a legitimate daytime bite, and it's built entirely around these mackerel schools stacking on the rips.

The pattern all week has been the same. Find the mackerel — and this year they've been sitting tight to structure, not spread out over open sand — then work the edges on the last hour of the ebb into slack. Peaked Hill Bars has been just as good as Race Point some mornings, maybe better on the smaller tides, because that structure holds bait even when the current's not ripping hard. Live mackerel under a balloon, freelined back with just enough weight to get it down eight or ten feet, has out-produced everything else. A couple of guys have done well slow-trolling umbrella rigs with mackerel-colored tubes through the same zones on the last of the incoming, but nothing's beaten a live bait doing what a live bait does when a big bass is sitting downcurrent with its mouth open.

Bluefish have been riding right alongside that bait, and they've been the more reliable fish this week if you just want steady action instead of waiting on one big bite. Sandy Neck has had bluefish blitzes most mornings on the outgoing tide, bunker and mackerel getting pushed up against the beach, birds working tight, blues in the eight-to-twelve-pound range hammering anything silver you throw at them — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, don't overthink it. That blitz pattern has been building all month and there's no sign of it backing off. If anything I'd expect it to keep spreading down toward Barnstable Harbor as more bait works its way along the beach.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, honestly, and I won't dress that up. The flats off Barnstable and around Sandy Neck channel have given up some nice fish to four and five pounds on white Gulp swimming mullets and bucktails, but you're working for them — long drifts, lots of empty stretches, then a flurry near a channel bend or a mussel bed where the current squeezes. Billingsgate has been quieter than I'd like for this time of year. The shoal itself is holding bait, but the fluke bite there has been more shorts than keepers. I think the water's still a touch cool on that structure for them to really set up in numbers — give it another couple weeks.

Cod are still mostly a story for later in the season out here, but we've started marking decent fish on the deeper humps north of Billingsgate, 90 to 110 feet, on the sonar during a couple of afternoon runs. Nothing worth targeting hard yet — one or two fish on diamond jigs when we dropped down out of curiosity — but that's usually how it starts. By late August, early September, that structure fills in and becomes a real fishery. Worth keeping in your back pocket if you're out there anyway working the bass.

Moon's building toward full in the first days of August, and that's going to matter. Current through these rips has been soft to moderate most of this week, which is part of why the bite windows have been short — twenty, thirty minutes around the slack when the mackerel bunch up and the bass move in to feed. As the tides build with the moon, I expect that window to widen and the current on Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars to sharpen up the whole pattern. If the mackerel stay put — and there's no reason to think they won't with water this cool holding steady — the next week should set up as well as anything we've had this summer. I'd be out there working the last of the ebb into slack, live mackerel rigged light, watching the birds and the meter before I ever drop a line.
